newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia's Kucan says parliament to meet Nov 28.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia's Kucan says parliament to meet Nov 28.

text.p: Slovenian President Milan Kucan said on Tuesday a first session of the country's newly-elected parliament would be held on November 28.

The president said he would choose a candidate for prime minister within 30 days of the first parliamentary session, during which time he would hold consultations with leaders of all parties which won seats to the 90-member parliament.
"I will name a candidate for prime minister according to the election result...and his chances of having enough support in parliament to form the government," Kucan told a news conference.

Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats emerged as the biggest single party with 25 seats in general elections on November 10, the second since Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia five years ago.
But Drnovsek has yet to enter talks with potential coalition candidates. A rightwing alliance of three parties won 45 seats, just one short of an absolute majority.
Drnovsek would have to persuade one or two of these parties to join a coalition with the Liberal Democrats to have any chance of running the next administration.

Kucan said all parliamentary parties would have to cooperate rather than emphasise their differences if Slovenia were to fulfil its aims of joining the European Union and NATO and completing the country's process of economic and social transformation.
Political analysts said forming the next government may take several weeks due to the knife-edge election result.
Kucan, a former Slovenian Communist Party leader widely respected for his part in the country's secession from Yugoslavia, was expected to lend his political weight to break the impasse.

The rightwing alliance known as the "Slovenian Spring" comprises the conservative People's Party and centre-right Social Democrats and Christian Democrats. The grouping hopes to be called on to form the next government with People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik as prime minister.
But Drnovsek has already stressed that his Liberal Democrats would take part in the new government only if he remained prime minister.
Slovenia boasts the highest GDP per capita among former communist countries, and hopes to join NATO by 1999 and the EU by 2001.
